links.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT vs gold clinical diagnosis and ophthalmologists
links.effect: Best F1 80.05% (Direct-English) vs ophthalmologists 89.35% and interns 82.69%; Chinese direct prompts 70.47%; VKH F1 0% in all prompts.
links.quote: From the perspective of clinical practice, ChatGPT’s diagnostic performance still did not reach the level of ophthalmologists or even ophthalmology interns.

links.outcome: Robustness of diagnostic performance to prompt language and prompt variation
links.effect: Chinese vs English prompts differed in recall (P=.03) and F1 (P=.04); mean F1 70.02% (Chinese) vs 76.47% (English).
links.quote: As shown in Table 4 , the results indicated significant differences in the recall ( P =.03) and F 1 -score ( P =.04) between Chinese and English prompts, while no significant difference was observed in the precision ( P =.18).

links.outcome: Performance on non-English (Chinese) prompts and reports versus English prompts
links.effect: Chinese prompts had 6.45% lower F1 than English; more incompleteness (63.53% vs 44.31%), hallucinations (5.88% vs 0.59%), misinformation (7.84% vs 1.96%).
links.quote: Also, analysis of the robustness of ChatGPT with different language prompts indicated significant differences in the recall (P=.03) and F1-score (P=.04) between Chinese and English prompts.

links.outcome: Rate of hallucinations and misinformation in ChatGPT reasoning on FFA reports
links.effect: Step-Chinese: hallucinations 5.88%, misinformation 7.84%; Step-English: 0.59% and 1.96%; 0.4 reasoning errors per report.
links.quote: Notably, although ChatGPT can derive a reasoning process to improve clinical interpretability, ophthalmologists identified some harmful mistakes, such as generating medical findings not mentioned in the original reports and quoting incorrect prior knowledge.

links.outcome: Performance gap across languages and disease categories due to English-centric training
links.effect: F1 fell 6.45% with Chinese prompts; VKH and CSC F1 under 4% vs DR/normal above 80%.
links.quote: The performance gap between different diseases and prompting strategies demonstrates the potential unfairness brought by the overrepresentation of the major diseases, languages, and countries.

links.outcome: Prompt-language robustness
links.effect: Mean (SD) F1 was 70.02% (3.54%) with Chinese prompts vs 76.47% (2.61%) with English prompts.
links.quote: The mean (SD) F 1 -scores of ChatGPT with Chinese and English prompts were 70.02% (3.54%) and 76.47% (2.61%), respectively.

links.outcome: Diagnostic performance versus clinicians
links.effect: Overall F1: ophthalmologists 89.35%, interns 82.69%, ChatGPT English prompts 76.76%, Chinese prompts 73.04%.
links.quote: Although ChatGPT performed better than experts for some disease types (eg, Direct-English and Step-English prompts for the normal and CRVO categories and all prompts for the BRVO category), the overall performance of ophthalmologists was the best (89.35%), followed by ophthalmology interns (82.69%), ChatGPT with Direct-English and Step-English prompts (76.76%), and ChatGPT with Direct-Chinese and Step-Chinese prompts (73.04%).

links.outcome: Retinal disease classification accuracy
links.effect: Direct-English achieved precision 79.61%, recall 83.12%, F1 80.05%; Direct-Chinese F1 was 9.58% lower.
links.quote: The Direct-English prompts achieved an overall precision of 79.61%, recall of 83.12%, and F 1 -score of 80.05%, which was 9.58% higher than that achieved by the Direct-Chinese prompts ( Table 2 ).

links.outcome: Performance by disease category
links.effect: Normal and DR F1 exceeded 80%, while VKH and CSC F1 were less than 4%.
links.quote: ChatGPT performed better in the normal and DR categories, with the F 1 -scores exceeding 80%, but performed worse in the VKH and CSC categories, achieving F 1 -scores of less than 4%.

links.outcome: Hallucinations and misinformation
links.effect: Step-English still had 44.31% incompleteness, 0.59% hallucinations, and 1.96% misinformation; Step-Chinese was higher, all P<.001.
links.quote: Although the average number of inference errors was similar (0.4 per report) between Step-Chinese and Step-English prompts ( P =.88, Wilcoxon rank-sum test), Step-English prompts brought less incompleteness (44.31%), hallucinations (0.59%), and misinformation (1.96%) (all P <.001, Chi-square test).
